---
title: "Group Assessment in an AI-Capable Cohort: Beyond the Presentation Assumption"
---

**Prepared by:** Michael Borck
**Purpose:** A position paper for staff designing or reviewing group assessments
**Companion to:** *Assessing AI Engagement: A Case for Moving Beyond Detection*

---

## Executive Summary

Group assessment is not inherently more AI-resistant than individual
assessment. The live presentation is widely assumed to be the strongest
safeguard, but it tests performance rather than understanding unless the Q&A is
designed to require genuine thinking. AI creates three new problems for group
work: the rewritten section problem, the free rider via AI problem, and a
sharpened attribution problem.

The strongest response is process infrastructure combined with a marks
structure that reflects how professional accountability works. Individual AI
conversation transcripts submitted alongside the group product make individual
engagement visible and scalable to assess. A marks structure weighted toward
individual process (illustratively 60-80%) over group product (20-40%) resolves
the free rider and attribution problems at once, mirrors real-world performance
review, and removes the most persistent source of student dissatisfaction with
group work.

Students should come to group work as individual contributors who collaborate,
which is what the workplace expects, rather than as members of a unit that
shares a single outcome.

---

## Introduction

Group assessment has always required students to balance individual
accountability against shared outcomes. AI does not create that tension, but it
sharpens it in ways existing frameworks were not designed to handle.

This paper argues for a marks structure and assessment design that reflect how
collaborative work functions in professional life. Students should come to group
work as individual contributors who collaborate, which is what the workplace
expects, rather than as members of a unit that shares a single outcome.
Assessment built that way is more resistant to AI misuse, and more honest
about what group work is for.

---

## The Presentation Assumption

Group assessment that culminates in a live presentation is widely assumed to be
more resistant to AI than individually submitted written work. The reasoning is
intuitive: students have to show up, speak, and respond to questions in real
time. AI cannot do that for them.

The assumption is partly right: a live presentation does require physical
presence and creates some opportunity for questions that test understanding
beyond a script. A group that has genuinely worked together tends to present
with a coherence that is difficult to fake.

A group can rehearse a scripted presentation to fluency in the same way an
individual can rehearse a video submission, and rehearsed fluency does not show
understanding under pressure. A marker watching a polished ten-minute
presentation cannot easily tell a group that built deep knowledge over several
weeks from one that spent two days rehearsing AI-generated content until it
sounded natural.

What a presentation tests depends almost entirely on whether it includes
genuine interrogation: questions the group could not have anticipated, asked in
a way that requires thinking rather than recall. Without that, a presentation
measures performance, and performance can be rehearsed.

---

## The Q&A as the Strongest Integrity Mechanism

If there is one design change worth prioritising in group presentations, it is
investing more in the Q&A than the presentation itself.

Questions that require understanding rather than retrieval are easy to
generate and hard to prepare for. Asking a group to apply their framework to an
unseen scenario, name the weakest assumption in their own argument, or argue
against their own conclusion shows whether they understand the material.

Distributing questions across group members at random, so no one knows in
advance who will answer what, adds another layer: a group that rehearsed
together without understanding the material will show it quickly.

This does not require a longer assessment session. Five minutes of genuine
interrogation reveals more than twenty minutes of polished presentation. The
weighting between the two in the marking rubric should reflect that.

---

## New Problems AI Creates for Group Work

AI introduces three integrity challenges that existing group assessment
frameworks were not designed to handle.

### The rewritten section problem

Students are reporting that group members rewrite each other's sections using
AI without consent. Traditional definitions of plagiarism and collusion do not
cover the practice, yet it undermines individual contribution in a way that is
hard to detect and currently sits in a grey area most academic integrity
policies do not address.

The student whose work was rewritten has a legitimate grievance: their
contribution has been replaced, their voice removed, and the group submission
no longer reflects their understanding. The student who rewrote it may have
believed they were helping. Neither peer review nor the final submission shows
what happened.

This needs explicit treatment in the team contract and in the unit's AI use
policy, as a collaboration ethics issue as well as an integrity one. Groups need
to agree upfront on what counts as editing versus replacing, and on what AI use
within a shared document is acceptable.

### The free rider via AI problem

Free riding in group work is not new. What is new is that AI lowers the cost
of a particular free riding strategy: a student who contributes nothing to the
thinking or research can generate a plausible-looking section at the last
minute. The output may be indistinguishable from genuine contribution in the
final submission.

Traditional free rider detection relies on peer assessment and process evidence.
AI makes the output signal less reliable, which places more weight on the
process signal. Weekly meeting records, contribution logs, and peer review
become more important in an AI-capable cohort.

### The attribution problem

Individual contribution has always been difficult to attribute in group work.
AI sharpens this in a specific way: a polished, well-structured section no
longer signals high individual effort. It may reflect comfort with AI tools, a
free rider with a good prompt, or genuine deep engagement expressed through an
AI-assisted drafting process. The output alone cannot tell you which. Attribution
requires process evidence, and process evidence requires infrastructure.

---

## Process Infrastructure as the Honest Response

AI in group assessment responds to the same fix as free riding and attribution
problems do: invest in process infrastructure instead of relying on the final
artefact to tell the whole story.

Useful process infrastructure includes:

- **Team contracts** agreed at the start, covering roles and timelines, plus
  explicit agreements about AI use within the group, what counts as individual
  contribution, and how disputes about rewriting will be handled
- **Weekly meeting records** submitted by the group, covering what was achieved,
  what is planned, and any issues arising. They create a paper trail that is
  hard to fabricate convincingly across a semester, and they surface problems
  early enough to address them
- **Individual contribution logs** or peer review instruments that ask what each
  member actually contributed, beyond whether they took part
- **A taught session on group work** that addresses AI use, the rewritten
  section problem, and what ethical collaboration looks like in practice.
  Students are rarely taught how to work in groups; they are placed in them and
  assessed on the outcome

None of this infrastructure is foolproof. A group that decides collectively to
game the process can do so. Explicit process scaffolding reduces complaints,
surfaces genuine problems earlier, and creates a more defensible record when
disputes arise.

---

## Individual AI Conversation Transcripts in Group Assessment

AI conversation transcripts used as an assessable component in individual
assessment carry over to group contexts with one addition: each member submits
their own transcript alongside the shared group product.

The group product alone cannot show individual engagement. Separate transcripts
show how members approached the same problem differently, which is evidence of
independent thinking, and they make retroactive fabrication hard: a convincing
individual transcript across a full semester requires the student to have
thought about the material throughout.

A transcript also captures the quality of the student's thinking, which peer
review misses, because it records what they asked rather than whether they
attended. Shallow one-shot questions show up, and so do iteration, pushback and
refinement.

For markers, the same signal-based approach from individual assessment applies.
Reviewing a one-page automated summary per student, covering prompt length,
number of turns, specificity over time, and evidence of pushback, is scalable
at group assessment sizes. The full transcript is available when a summary flags
something worth examining more closely.

The process artefacts described here replace other marking mechanisms rather
than adding to them. Individual transcripts remove the need to adjudicate peer
review disputes after the fact, and automated summaries with selective deep
dives take less time than resolving a formal misconduct complaint. Surfacing
engagement problems early in the semester, through weekly meeting records and
contribution logs, reduces the disputes that consume the most marking time. The
net workload is manageable when the infrastructure is set up at the start of
semester rather than retrofitted at submission time.

The approach also assumes students know how to engage productively with AI:
iterating, pushing back and refining a prompt instead of accepting the first
output. If they have not been taught these skills, a process mark penalises low
AI literacy rather than low intellectual effort. Building basic AI engagement
skills early in the unit, through a taught session or a structured early task,
is a prerequisite for fairness. Staff looking for support can draw on the AI
Skills Passport resources developed for the school.

### A Group AI Reflection as a Bridging Component

Individual transcripts capture each member's thinking process, and the group
product captures the shared outcome. A short Group AI Reflection submitted
alongside both adds a useful middle step.

It asks the group to answer one question together: how did you decide which
AI-generated ideas to keep, which to discard, and why? To answer it, the group
has to discuss the AI-generated content rather than divide it up and assemble
the parts. That shows whether the group made sense of the material together or
simply submitted separately.

The reflection need not be long. Half a page, or a short segment in the
presentation, is enough to make the link between individual process and shared
product visible and assessable.

---

## Marks Structure: From Combined vs Differentiated to Process vs Product

Group assessments typically split between a combined group mark and a
differentiated individual mark. AI sharpens the weakness in both.

A combined group mark makes individual engagement invisible: a student who
contributed nothing but generated a polished section with AI receives the same
mark as one who did the intellectual work. A differentiated mark tries to fix
this but needs reliable attribution, which AI complicates, because a polished
section no longer signals individual effort.

Both problems point toward the same solution: stop trying to attribute the
product and start assessing the process instead. A structure worth considering:

- **Individual process mark (illustratively 60-80%):** each student's AI conversation transcript,
  quality of prompting, evidence of critical engagement, and demonstrated
  personal understanding of the group's work
- **Group product mark (illustratively 20-40%):** the shared artefact, presentation, or report,
  assessed as a team

This shifts the incentives. Students have a reason to engage deeply with the
material themselves, because that is where most of the marks sit, and the group
product becomes the synthesis of that engagement rather than a
division-of-labour exercise assembled at the last minute.

A student who contributes nothing cannot fabricate a detailed individual
transcript across a full semester, and attribution no longer turns on who wrote
which paragraph but on what each individual contributed to the thinking.

### This mirrors how the real world actually works

In professional life, nobody receives a group performance review. Every
individual is assessed on their contribution, their thinking, and their ability
to work effectively with others. Good managers evaluate team members the same
way this structure does: the team delivered the product (30%), but what did you
specifically bring to it and how did you think through the problems (70%)?

Students who understand the framing from the start approach group work
differently, as individual contributors who collaborate.

The 70/30 split also removes a persistent source of dissatisfaction with group
work: the feeling that someone else's lack of effort affects your mark. Under
this structure your mark is mostly yours, which reflects how contribution and
accountability work in professional life. Students tend to recognise the
fairness when it is explained at the start.

---

## What Genuine Engagement Looks Like in a Group Context

The engagement spectrum from individual assessment applies at the group level,
but the social context creates additional pressures. A group whose members
discuss ideas, challenge each other's contributions and build on each other's
thinking produces something different from one that divides the work, completes
sections separately and assembles them at the end. The final product may look
the same; the process is different.

Signals worth looking for in process evidence:

- Do the weekly meeting records show genuine discussion of ideas or just task
  allocation?
- Do individual peer reviews show awareness of what other members actually
  contributed, or are they generic?
- In the presentation Q&A, can members speak to each other's sections, or only
  their own?
- Does the team contract show evidence of genuine negotiation, or does it look
  like a template completed in five minutes?

None of these signals is definitive on its own. Together they give a clearer
picture of group engagement than the final submitted artefact alone.

---

## What the Marker Sees: A Brief Vignette

Consider two versions of the same group assessment. In the first, the marker
receives a polished twelve-page report and a twenty-minute presentation. Three
of the four sections are well-structured and confidently delivered. One member
is vague under questioning. The marker suspects uneven contribution but has
nothing concrete to point to.

In the second version, the marker receives the same report and presentation,
plus four individual transcripts, four brief reflections on key moments, and a
one-paragraph Group AI Reflection explaining why the group rejected two of the
AI's initial framework suggestions. The automated summary shows one member's
prompts were consistently short and generic while the others' became more
specific over time. The marker knows where to look, what questions to ask, and
has defensible evidence whatever the outcome.

The group product is identical in both versions; what the marker can see is
not.

---

## Summary

Group assessment is not inherently more AI-resistant than individual assessment.
The presentation assumption offers partial protection, and the Q&A carries more
integrity weight than the presentation itself.

AI creates three new problems: the rewritten section problem, the free rider
via AI problem, and a sharpened attribution problem. All three point in the same
direction: process infrastructure matters more in an AI-capable cohort.

A group that decides to perform engagement rather than demonstrate it can do
so. Weekly meeting records can be written after the fact, peer reviews can be
generic, and transcripts can be crafted to look iterative. No infrastructure is
foolproof. Process evidence can be faked, but faking it convincingly across a
semester takes more effort than genuine engagement, and the signals above make
unconvincing fabrication visible to an attentive marker.

Individual AI conversation transcripts submitted alongside the group product
make individual engagement visible, scalable to assess, and difficult to
fabricate retroactively.

A marks structure weighted toward individual process over group product resolves
the combined versus differentiated mark dilemma, mirrors real-world professional
accountability, and removes the persistent student dissatisfaction that comes
from shared marks for unequal effort.

The goal remains the same as in individual assessment: assess where on the
engagement spectrum students operated, not whether they used AI. In a group
context, that question has both a group-level and an individual-level answer,
and good assessment design surfaces both.
